kurz: Four use cases in which options make sense, why other uses mainly cost money and how the multiplier determines the portfolio size required.

bloecke.md:
Options do not generate return; they reshape risk. The buyer pays a certain small amount and in return receives an uncertain large chance. The option writer does the opposite deal. They collect the small payment with certainty and in return may have to make a large payment. Before costs, the options market is a zero-sum game between two parties. After spread, fees and taxes, the result for private investors as a whole is negative. An option therefore only makes sense if it creates a risk profile that could not be created with shares and cash alone, and if this profile is worth the price. That is the only reliable rule for using options.

This rules out the most common motive. Investors who merely expect a security to rise do not need an option. It is enough for them to hold more of that security. The leverage of an option costs time value, and time value inevitably falls to zero by expiry. Raising the equity allocation from 60% to 75%, by contrast, costs nothing. Anyone who implements the same view with purchased calls pays premium and spread. In addition, they are betting that the movement will occur in time before expiry. With options, being right about the direction and still losing money is the normal case.

bloecke.md:
## Sensible use cases

One viable use case is hedging a cluster risk. Employees who may not sell employee shares because of a lock-up period, for example, have a risk with a date, as do investors who need a fixed amount from the portfolio in twelve months. A put is designed for such cases. Its costs must be factored in fully. A permanent hedge over years costs premium every year and thus a considerable part of the equity return. Hedging therefore makes sense for a specific occasion with a fixed date, but not as a permanent state.

Another use case is the premium for an obligation that you would take on anyway. A cash-secured put is the commitment to buy a share at the strike price. The seller receives a premium for this. A covered call is the commitment to hand over holdings at the strike price. Both positions are justifiable as long as the commitment is meant seriously, that is, the money is ready or the shares may be handed over. In both cases, the premium is not additional income without anything in return. The seller gives up part of their own opportunity for it.

Finally, a movement you can specify can be captured with capped risk. If you can state which security should move by how much and by when, you can use a vertical spread for this. The maximum loss is fixed in euros as soon as the position is opened. The same applies to purchased warrants and knock-outs, where at most the purchase price can be lost.

All other uses, such as betting on quarterly results, the weekly call far out of the money or uncovered option writing, are not sensible applications. They mainly generate costs and only occasionally produce a lucky hit.

bloecke.md:
## Minimum capital and multiplier

The entry threshold results from the contract size and not from the premium. A share option usually covers 100 shares. At a price of €200, a single contract thus controls €20,000 of [[Notional value|notional value]]. Index contracts are even larger. The DAX closed at 25,717 points on 17 September 2026, and the regular DAX future is based on €25 per index point. One contract therefore corresponds to around €643,000. For the mini contract with €5 per point it is around €129,000, and for the micro contract with €1 per point around €26,000.

This results in a fixed lower limit. For covered positions, you need either 100 units of an underlying or the strike price in cash, so €9,500 for a commitment at €95. This money is then unavailable for anything else for a year. A portfolio of €5,000 could only enter into such a commitment uncovered, and uncovered positions are the wrong way to go. Covered, it would only work with underlyings below €50, and even then a large part of the portfolio would be tied up in a single position. For a single option position not to make up half the portfolio straight away, sums in the mid five figures are realistically needed. Even then, only underlyings in the lower price range or spreads come into question.

bloecke.md:
## Stake and risk

The costliest error of reasoning arises when looking at the account display. When you buy an option, it shows the purchase price, and that is the full risk, because no more than the premium can be lost. When you sell, it shows a credit and a margin requirement, and neither figure says anything about the loss scenario. The margin is collateral that Eurex Clearing recalculates daily on a portfolio basis. It rises as soon as the position goes badly. The position size is therefore based on the maximum loss in a stress scenario, never on premium or margin.

The following illustrative calculation compares three ways of implementing the same view, plus buying the shares. The view is that the share will not fall below €95 in the next 30 days. The assumptions are a price of the underlying of €100, an implied volatility of 25%, an interest rate of 2% and a contract size of 100. The prices are calculated using Black-Scholes.

bloecke.titel: Capital tied up and maximum loss compared
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. With the spread and the share purchase, stake and risk are the same figure; with the uncovered short put, the maximum loss is just over six times as high as the margin.

bloecke.md: The short put 95 brings in €93 of premium and requires €1,500 of margin in the illustrative calculation. This assumes 15% of the notional value, because there are no fixed rates in risk-based margin models. If the share falls to €60, the loss is (95 − 60) × 100 − 93 = €3,407. That is more than twice the amount deposited. At the same time, the margin requirement rises in the middle of the price slide, which leads to a forced close-out at the most unfavourable point. For uncovered option writers, such a course of events is the rule. Many small gains are set against rare, very large losses.

A share is at €100, the results are due the next morning, and the implied volatility of the at-the-money call with 14 days to expiry is 60%. The call costs €4.72 per share, that is, €472 per contract.

After publication, the uncertainty about the results has been removed. Implied volatility falls to 28%, and the remaining term to 13 days. The share has risen by 3% to €103, so the direction was right.

The call is now quoted at €4.02. That corresponds to a loss of 15% despite the right direction. The arithmetical break-even is around €103.94. If the price rise stays below just under 4%, the position loses, even though the share moves in the expected direction. What was mainly paid for at purchase was the high volatility, and it was at its most expensive on the day before publication. (Illustrative calculation using Black-Scholes, interest rate 2%, excluding dividends and costs.)

- Calculate the loss in euros that arises if the underlying moves 30% against the position, and check whether the account can bear it.
- Clarify whether, in the event of early assignment, the shares are ready in the portfolio or the money is ready in the account.
- Assess whether implied volatility is high or low relative to its own history, and check whether the position is on the matching side.
- Decide how the position will be closed if the market can only be traded with wide spreads for a week.

If one of these points cannot be clarified with figures, the planned position is still based on a guess.

## Tax treatment

Since the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024, the most serious tax objection to options in Germany has fallen away. The €20,000 annual cap on offsetting losses from derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) under Section 20(6) sentence 5 EStG (Income Tax Act), old version, was abolished without replacement, with effect for all open cases (Section 52(28) EStG). Losses from derivative transactions therefore go into the general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf) and may also be offset there against gains from share sales. The statutory special pot only concerns losses from sales of shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG).

The other rules continue to apply. Option writer premiums are capital income under Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG, and gains from derivative transactions under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG. They are taxed at 25% plus solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total (Section 32d(1) EStG). There is no partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) as there is for equity funds. Losses from capital assets remain confined to their own offsetting category and can only be carried forward. The [[Premium yield|premium yield]] of a cash-secured put, €93 on €9,500 of capital tied up, corresponds to 0.98% in 30 days. Annualised, this would look like 12.6%. After flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer), around 9.1% of that remains. This extrapolation assumes that the rare large movement never comes. The premium, however, is paid as compensation for the risk of this very movement. This presentation is not tax advice; the legal position is as of September 2026.

Options are not an entry-level instrument, nor are they a hallmark of advanced investors. They presuppose that an emergency reserve, freedom from expensive debt and a broadly diversified core portfolio are already in place, because they improve none of these three points. If you want to learn to use them nonetheless, the sensible start is covered positions on an underlying you would hold anyway. The position should be so small that a total loss does not noticeably change the portfolio.

mitnehmen: An option is only the right tool if it creates a risk profile that cannot be created with shares and cash.
For a pure directional view without a date, the equity allocation is the cheaper instrument, because it costs no time value.
The entry threshold is determined by the multiplier, that is, 100 shares per contract or €25 per DAX point in the regular future.
Margin and premium do not show the risk, so the position size is based on the maximum loss in a stress scenario.
With purchased options, a loss despite the right direction is the normal case, because what you pay for is the volatility and not the view.

begriffe.text: The value of the underlying that a contract controls, that is, contract size times price, or for index contracts, multiplier times index level. Risk is measured by the notional value and not by premium or margin.

A sold option for which the corresponding holding or cash amount is missing. The premium is the same as for the covered variant, and for the put so is the loss potential. With the uncovered call, by contrast, the loss is theoretically unlimited, and on assignment the cover is missing.
The fall in implied volatility after a scheduled event such as quarterly results. It reduces the value of purchased options regardless of the direction of the price.
The premium collected in relation to the capital tied up for it. Annualising it assumes that the rare large loss never occurs.
